hypothesis: An exact target-relative continuation-cost controller can distinguish recovery, terminal structural obstruction, and finite budget infeasibility while returning a minimum-worst-case-cost next experiment; immediate target-pair gain is not universally cost-optimal.

controls.description: A non-memoized recursive enumeration must agree with the memoized dynamic program on every registered finite system.
The exact policy tree accounts for every candidate world as the hidden actual world and verifies target-correct recovery or a valid terminal obstruction.
Target-equal, transcript-inconsistent, unknown-world, and forged-separator certificates must fail closed.
Root recovery, terminal impossibility, and finite over-budget recovery produce three distinct statuses.
World, target, and experiment relabeling preserve costs; a duplicate experiment cannot improve the optimum.
The benchmark verifies that the local COGR synthesis and repaired-prior erratum preserve the L1 null rather than transporting failed geometry as support.

gates.criterion: Every finite task has aligned nonempty worlds, outcomes, targets, permitted experiments, and positive integer costs.
Memoized and independent exact worst-case costs agree on all 500,912 systems.
Every one of 1,975,104 hidden-world episodes ends in target-correct recovery or a valid terminal obstruction.
Every emitted terminal certificate validates and every registered invalid mutation is rejected.
Exact worst-case cost is no greater than target-greedy, all-pair-greedy, or fixed-order cost on every recoverable system.
Recovery, terminal obstruction, and finite budget infeasibility remain distinct outcomes.
Relabeling preserves policy costs and a redundant experiment cannot lower the exact optimum.
A strict greedy counterexample is replayable, or the paper reports a bounded null and withholds universal optimality.
The paper preserves the COGR learned-geometry KILL and makes no positive concern-geometry claim.
The manifest, source digest, results, counterexample fixture, tests, paper, and PDF are replayable public artifacts.
